entries.effect: The account route to the robot's local password fails for any client on this network: this is its first call. Get the password before blocking it.
The iRobot sign-in (/v2/login) that returns the robot list and local password fails on this network.
The Gigya identity sign-in that starts the account route fails on this network.

No update reaches the oven. The same service was the only known way to finish first boot on a factory-reset oven, which needs a cloud download to get there; the service retired on 2026-09-22, so the block now costs nothing that has not already gone — and a June oven should not be factory-reset either way.
As for dev-devices-ota.junelife.com: no update reaches the oven.

Remote control, camera stills, guided cooks and push notifications stop, as they did for everyone at the 2026-09-22 shutdown. The oven still cooks from its touchscreen. Production updates were offered in-band on this channel, so blocking it also stops the offer.

The TV cannot check for firmware. A pending-update prompt may still appear at every boot (reported with the Homebrew Channel's hosts-file block on, which one tester says applies only after the boot-time check): decline it, and keep the TV's own automatic updates off.
No firmware image can be fetched from this name.
No firmware image can be fetched from this name.

The TV takes its clock from this service — a header on its HTTPS API rather than NTP — and the Content Store, app updates and home-screen configuration live here too. Blocked, the clock resets after a cold boot (to 2019-12-31 on one report) and apps then fail their certificate checks.
The newer SDP family: blocking it is reported to stop the TV setting its clock and to disable the Content Store.
Content Store icons and screenshots, EULA acceptance and app downloads fail.
The TV's internet-connection check fails and it reports itself offline. One list's author says it must stay reachable; other lists block it. What else follows from a failed check is not documented.
Ads in the home screen and Content Store stop; community reports find nothing else breaks.
Home-screen recommendation and promotion rows stop loading. The beacon and crash-upload services here go with them; nothing else is reported to break.

Off-LAN control through the Kasa app, Alexa and Google Assistant stops, and so do app-driven updates. On a set of 2023 builds a device that cannot reach its cloud also drops and rejoins Wi-Fi every 10 minutes: TP-Link lists KP125/EP25 1.0.10, EP40A 1.0.5, KP303 v2 1.0.7, HS103 v5 1.0.8, HS200 v5 1.0.10, HS210 v3 1.0.9, HS220 v3 1.0.10, KS200 1.0.5 and KS220 1.0.9, and says fixed builds have shipped — which fixes it only by taking an update.
entries.workaround: Unbind the device first (cnCloud.unbind, or smartlife.iot.common.cloud.unbind on a bulb) — it needs the cloud reachable, so do it before blocking. It stopped the reconnect loop for one owner, though an HS220 on 1.0.10 kept looping until the fixed build. Failing that, resolve this name to a LAN machine that accepts the TCP connection instead of to a null address; a device answered that way was reported to settle where a refused one did not.

entries.effect: The US regional form of n-devs.tplinkcloud.com, with the same cost: off-LAN control, voice assistants and app-driven updates stop, and the 2023 builds listed there reconnect Wi-Fi every 10 minutes.
entries.workaround: As for n-devs.tplinkcloud.com: unbind before blocking, or answer the connection on the LAN.

entries.effect: Off-LAN control through the Kasa app and voice assistants stops; the device keeps retrying, and the Kasa app on the LAN shows it as "local only".
TP-Link staff say an HS103 (hardware 2, firmware 1.1.2) must be able to resolve this name and deventry.tplinkcloud.com; what fails when it cannot is not stated.
TP-Link staff say an HS103 (hardware 2, firmware 1.1.2) must be able to resolve this name and devs-gw.tplinkcloud.com; what fails when it cannot is not stated.

No image can be fetched from here, so an update ordered through the app or the cloud fails to download. The cloud hands the device the URL, so an image served from any other host would get past this — no source has tested the block itself, which is why the firewall rule stays the recommendation.

Schedules, timers and away mode run on the device's clock, and there is no battery-backed clock: after a power cut the device keeps a default time (an HS100 wakes in January 2000) until something sets it.
entries.workaround: Resolve the name to a LAN NTP server (DHCP's NTP option is not known to reach the device), or set the clock over the local protocol — time.set_timezone, or python-kasa's `kasa time sync`.

entries.effect: As for pool.ntp.org: schedules, timers and away mode drift or stop once the clock is lost.
entries.workaround: Resolve the name to a LAN NTP server, or set the clock over the local protocol.

entries.effect: The Kasa app loses its cloud sign-in and device list on this network. The device is unaffected.
As for wap.tplinkcloud.com: the app's cloud side, not the device's.

profiles.cloud: Every host the device itself contacts, except time sources. The DNS half of cutting the device off from its vendor; the firewall rule is the other half.
profiles.updates: Firmware update hosts only, so the rest of the vendor cloud, and the vendor app away from home, usually keeps working; where a device's update offer rides its main cloud link, that link is listed too. It stops the update hosts the specs NAME; vendors move update traffic without notice, so this is the weakest list here.
